title: From Merchant Correspondence to AI Platforms: Technology, Infrastructure and Business by Era

paras: A continuous account of how information speed, computing architecture, network ownership and revenue models transformed global business.

Before electrical telegraphy, merchants, bankers and governments depended on couriers, ships, postal systems, printed price lists and trusted correspondents. A transaction across distant cities required physical transport of information. Faster access to reliable commercial intelligence could confer an advantage in trading and finance. Governments controlled or licensed many routes and postal services, while private merchants and banks maintained correspondence networks.

Worked example: A merchant seeking to buy goods overseas sends a letter specifying price and quantity. The message travels with a ship; the reply may arrive weeks later. Capital is committed while prices and supply conditions can change. Faster communication reduces some information delay but does not eliminate transport, credit or counterparty risk.

blocks.h2: 2. Telegraph: information begins to outrun goods
paras: Electrical signaling moved messages across wire networks far faster than physical couriers. Telegraph offices, railway lines, submarine cables, repeaters and standardized procedures formed an early communications infrastructure. Operators earned message tariffs and cable charges; financial institutions and news agencies benefited from more timely information. International agreements addressed compatibility, tariffs and administrative procedures. Public and private ownership coexisted.

blocks.h2: 3. Telephone, radio and public utility systems
paras: Telephone exchanges enabled interactive voice communication, while radio created new broadcasting and wireless signaling systems. Manual and later automatic switches, long-distance trunk lines, broadcast transmitters, spectrum allocation and submarine cable networks required large investments. In different countries, operators ranged from state administrations to private firms with exclusive or regulated franchises. Revenue included subscriptions, metered calls, leased circuits and advertising-supported broadcasting.

Electronic digital computers used vacuum tubes and later transistors and integrated circuits to process discrete information. Batch processing, stored-program designs, magnetic storage and early operating systems enabled organizations to process payroll, inventory and financial records at scale. Time-sharing allowed multiple users to share costly computing systems. Mainframe-centered architectures linked terminals to centralized processors; the terminal was often an input/output device rather than an independent personal computer.

blocks.h2: 5. Packet networks, the Internet and Web generations
paras: Terminology: “Web 0” is an informal retrospective label. Web 1.0 and 2.0 describe broad usage patterns, not formal protocol versions. “Web3” commonly refers to blockchain-based systems, whereas the Semantic Web has also been called “Web 3.0” in other contexts. Web 4.0 and Web 5.0 have no single universally adopted technical definition.

blocks.h2: 6. Servers, operating systems and networks become software-managed
paras: Dedicated servers evolved into shared mainframes, time-sharing, hardware virtualization, cloud VMs, containers and orchestrated services. LANs and leased WANs were complemented by VPNs, VLANs, software-defined networking and cloud virtual networks. Businesses adopted ERP, electronic payments, APIs and SaaS. A virtual machine is an isolated guest computing environment; a container is an isolated process environment sharing a kernel; a virtual network is a software-defined abstraction that still uses physical links and devices.

blocks.h2: 7. 2026: AI infrastructure builds on all previous layers
paras: Modern AI systems depend on semiconductor design, manufacturing capacity, electrical power, data centers, fiber links, network routing, operating systems, container scheduling, storage, model software and distribution channels. Revenue may accrue to chip suppliers, data-center operators, cloud platforms, model providers, application developers and integrators. Governments continue to influence trade, energy, privacy, procurement, safety and competition rules.
References support the institutional background and technical definitions. Interpretive comparisons and illustrative models are identified as analysis rather than established causal findings.
